chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ibrahim, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), that he was asked about a tree whose trunk is in the Haram (sanctuary) and its branches are in the Hal (permissible area); a bird on one of its branches was shot by a man and fell.
He (peace be upon him) said: 'The penalty is upon him if its trunk is in the Haram.'

And it is not permissible for the Muhrim (one in Ihram) to say 'Labbayk' (responding to the call of Hajj/Umrah) to one who calls him as long as he is in Ihram, but rather he should answer him with words other than that. Narrated.

key_terms.الْحَرَم: The sacred sanctuary (e.g., Mecca), where specific rules apply
key_terms.الْحِل: The permissible area outside the sacred sanctuary
key_terms.جَزَاء: Penalty or compensation (for breaking Ihram or hunting)
key_terms.لُبِّي: To say 'Labbayk', the ritual response used in Hajj/Umrah
key_terms.مُحْرِم: A pilgrim in the state of Ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on shooting a bird from a tree that straddles the boundary of the Haram?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq clarifies the spatial extent of the Haram's sanctity, ruling that a bird perched on branches extending from a Haram-rooted tree is subject to the full penalty, illustrating the principle of 'extending the boundary' in ritual law. Additionally, it distinguishes between the formal ritual response 'Labbayk' and casual speech, ensuring the pilgrim maintains the integrity of their Ihram state without unnecessary verbal ritualization. These rulings highlight the precision required in maintaining the sacred state during Hajj.
